prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

Paths and paved areas in roadside green spaces shall meet the following requirements: 1. The material and thickness of the paving surface layer shall be coordinated with the road greening style and use function, and integrated with sponge city design. Ecological permeable materials should be used where possible, with anti-slip functions, and polished surface materials shall not be used. 2. Paved areas should have shading measures, and the shaded area in summer should preferably be greater than 50% of the recreational activity area. 1.4.1 Paving Style and Color 1. Quality improvement of non-motorized vehicle lane paving In riverside greenways and other leisure spaces, or at locations with a significantly high incidence of traffic accidents involving motor vehicles and non-motorized vehicles, non-motorized vehicle lanes may use colored paving. Isolation facilities may be appropriately arranged to improve the cycling experience for non-motorized vehicles. Figure 1.4-1 Schematic diagram of non-motorized vehicle lane paving 2. Quality improvement of sidewalk paving 11 A. Traffic-function roads The sides of traffic-function roads are mainly non-open interfaces, with relatively few non-traffic activities, and the paved areas mainly serve traffic distribution functions. Paving design shall implement the concepts of safety, health, comfort, and people-oriented design. Figure 1.4-2 Example of paving for traffic-function roads B. Living-service roads The activity groups on living-service roads include residents and workers around the road, as well as people from other areas who come for shopping and strolling. In terms of paving materials, color, texture, and grain, attention shall be paid to people’s perceptions, and localized creative design shall be applied to road entrances to enrich the walking experience. Figure 1.4-3 Example of paving for living-service roads C. Scenic leisure roads According to the characteristics of scenic leisure roads and the behavioral characteristics of the activity groups, the design objective of the paved area is to provide a safe, comfortable slow-traffic environment and leisure space. The paving surface layer shall use natural, aesthetically pleasing, comfortable, and ecological materials, while also meeting the requirement of coordination with the surrounding landscape. 12 Figure 1.4-4 Example of paving for scenic leisure roads D. Historic-style streets and lanes The paving design of historic-style streets and lanes shall continue and reflect cultural charm and local character, and shape distinctive spaces. Road design should focus on creating a historical and cultural atmosphere. The paving materials and texture shall be integrated with the surrounding environment. Figure 1.4-5 Example of paving for historic-style streets and lanes E. Comprehensive roads Comprehensive roads have a relatively high degree of mixing in road functions and interface types. They shall take into account the different needs of multiple characteristics, optimize the slow-traffic travel experience, consider the composite needs of road functions and the businesses on both sides, and create a paving system that is highly adaptable and simple and elegant. Figure 1.4-6 Example of paving for comprehensive roads F. Smart city demonstration roads No special requirements

Roundabouts** A. Conventional roundabouts should not be used at urban arterial road intersections. For roads approaching an intersection on a grade, when the longitudinal gradient is ≥3%, a roundabout at-grade intersection should not be adopted. Roundabout at-grade intersections shall not be used on expressways or on major arterials with heavy traffic volumes. B. The number of motor-vehicle lanes in the roundabout should preferably be arranged as 2 to 3 lanes. For the reconstruction of existing large roundabouts or where special needs exist, the requirements may be relaxed. **2.2.6 Sight Distance Requirements** Landscaping and greenery within the sight triangle of at-grade intersections shall remain visually open and unobstructed. Obstacles that obstruct the driver’s line of sight within the sight triangle of an at-grade intersection shall be removed. Greenery higher than 1.2 m that obstructs the driver’s line of sight is not permitted. **2.3 Grade-separated Intersections** When expressways intersect with urban roads of all classes, grade-separated intersections must be adopted; when expressways intersect with expressways, grade-separated intersections must be adopted; when expressways intersect with arterial roads, grade-separated intersections shall be adopted. The conditions for setting up grade-separated crossings between roads and railways are as follows: A. Grade-separated intersections must be provided where expressways cross railways. B. Grade-separated intersections shall be provided where arterial roads, secondary arterial roads, and branch roads cross railways and where traffic volume at the crossing is high or railway shunting operations are frequent and the cumulative closure time of the crossing is long. C. Grade-separated intersections shall be provided where arterial roads and secondary arterial roads cross railways and where, during peak road traffic periods, long single-closure periods occur frequently. D. Grade-separated intersections shall be provided where roads used by trams or trolleybuses cross railways. 35 **2.4 Roads** **2.4.1 New Construction Projects** Urban road traffic design shall follow the following principles: 1. People-oriented: importance shall be attached to the functional requirements of urban roads in shaping the environment and enhancing road vitality, and importance shall be attached to road landscape design with natural and humanistic features to create a pleasant road traffic environment. 2. System coordination: the designed road shall be incorporated into the overall urban road network, with full consideration of land-use functions and traffic characteristics within the road influence area, so as to achieve integration and coordination between land use functions and the transport system. 3. Functional matching: due consideration shall be given to the various use functions and attributes of roads, and the functional spatial requirements of various transport modes in the higher-level plan shall be coordinated and implemented, while meeting the needs of public activity space. 4. Safety and order: traffic safety hazards shall be reduced through facility layout, engineering, and management measures, with particular emphasis on protecting vulnerable road users such as pedestrians and cyclists, and ensuring orderly traffic flow. 5. The setting of walkway lights and streetlights shall take the intersection stop line as the starting and ending point, at a distance of 3.0 m–10.0 m. Figure 4.3-4 Example of Walkway Lights 4.3.3 Pavement Surfacing 1. Sidewalk paving: It shall meet the requirements of stability, anti-slip performance, flatness, ecological environmental protection, and urban landscape. Its design shall be practical, economical, aesthetically pleasing, and durable, and shall be designed for permeability in accordance with sponge city requirements. Guidance and directional signs may be added to the paving; signs shall be appropriately scaled and clearly informative. 2. Tactile paving: The color of tactile paving should contrast with the color of adjacent sidewalk paving and be coordinated with the surrounding landscape. The surface of tactile paving profiles shall have anti-slip functionality. The width should be 0.3 m–0.6 m, and the tactile pattern shall protrude 4 mm above the road surface. Tactile paving shall be laid continuously and shall avoid obstacles such as trees (tree pits), utility poles, and guy wires. Figure 4.3-5 Example of tactile paving 3. Curb stones: These shall be designed in accordance with road class, construction scale, landscape environment, and usage requirements. Sidewalks must be provided with curb ramps at all intersections and at the entrances/exits of residential communities and institutions fronting the street. The height difference between the curb stone and the road surface shall not exceed 1 cm. At pedestrian crossings, the centerline of the curb-ramp opening should align with the centerline of the crosswalk. At road intersections, curb ramps are recommended to adopt a full-width, single-sided ramp descending to the bottom. 4. Tree pits / tree grates: Their dimensions shall be designed in coordination with the sidewalk paving, forming a certain proportional modular relationship. The paved surface of the tree pit / tree grate should be flush with the sidewalk paving. Tree grates should preferably use fiberglass grating, eco-friendly rubber, stone paving, and similar materials. In parks, squares, commercial pedestrian streets, and other leisure activity areas, tree pits should be designed in combination with seating, or as compact / multifunctional designs that provide seating functions. Figure 4.3-6 Example of tree pits / tree grates 5. Manhole covers: All types of manhole covers shall comply with the relevant standards in Manhole Covers (GB/T 23858-2009). The paved surface of the manhole cover shall be flush with the sidewalk paving surface, and the height difference shall not exceed 1 cm. Concealed manhole covers may be used; the decorative surface layer shall be unified with the road paving. Manhole covers with distinctive patterns may also be used. Figure 4.3-7 Example of manhole covers 4.3.4 Information service facilities Information service facilities refer to service facilities that provide information on roads, places, public announcements, and similar matters within an area. prompt_c3:
As a city streetscape evaluation expert, please analyze the uploaded streetscape image based on the specified persona perspective and evaluation indicators, and return a JSON result.
 Persona Selection
Road User Type
- All Road Users
- Pedestrians
- Cyclists
- Drivers
Socially Vulnerable Groups
- All Social Groups
- Persons with Disabilities
- Adolescents (<18)
- Older Adults (≥60)
Current Selection:
All Road Users; All Social Groups
 Indicator Selection
Justice
- Equity
- Fairness
- Accessibility
Safety
Livability
Sustainability
Aesthetics
Comfort
- Thermal Comfort
- Physical Comfort
- Psychological Comfort
Walkability
Bikeability
Selected Indicators:
Justice; Safety; Livability; Sustainability; Aesthetics; Comfort; Walkability
 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.
 4. Output Format Requirements (Return JSON ONLY, no extra text):

Roundabouts** A. Conventional roundabouts should not be used at urban arterial road intersections. For roads approaching an intersection on a grade, when the longitudinal gradient is ≥3%, a roundabout at-grade intersection should not be adopted. Roundabout at-grade intersections shall not be used on expressways or on major arterials with heavy traffic volumes. B. The number of motor-vehicle lanes in the roundabout should preferably be arranged as 2 to 3 lanes. For the reconstruction of existing large roundabouts or where special needs exist, the requirements may be relaxed. **2.2.6 Sight Distance Requirements** Landscaping and greenery within the sight triangle of at-grade intersections shall remain visually open and unobstructed. Obstacles that obstruct the driver’s line of sight within the sight triangle of an at-grade intersection shall be removed. Greenery higher than 1.2 m that obstructs the driver’s line of sight is not permitted. **2.3 Grade-separated Intersections** When expressways intersect with urban roads of all classes, grade-separated intersections must be adopted; when expressways intersect with expressways, grade-separated intersections must be adopted; when expressways intersect with arterial roads, grade-separated intersections shall be adopted. The conditions for setting up grade-separated crossings between roads and railways are as follows: A. Grade-separated intersections must be provided where expressways cross railways. B. Grade-separated intersections shall be provided where arterial roads, secondary arterial roads, and branch roads cross railways and where traffic volume at the crossing is high or railway shunting operations are frequent and the cumulative closure time of the crossing is long. C. Grade-separated intersections shall be provided where arterial roads and secondary arterial roads cross railways and where, during peak road traffic periods, long single-closure periods occur frequently. D. Grade-separated intersections shall be provided where roads used by trams or trolleybuses cross railways. 35 **2.4 Roads** **2.4.1 New Construction Projects** Urban road traffic design shall follow the following principles: 1. People-oriented: importance shall be attached to the functional requirements of urban roads in shaping the environment and enhancing road vitality, and importance shall be attached to road landscape design with natural and humanistic features to create a pleasant road traffic environment. 2. System coordination: the designed road shall be incorporated into the overall urban road network, with full consideration of land-use functions and traffic characteristics within the road influence area, so as to achieve integration and coordination between land use functions and the transport system. 3. Functional matching: due consideration shall be given to the various use functions and attributes of roads, and the functional spatial requirements of various transport modes in the higher-level plan shall be coordinated and implemented, while meeting the needs of public activity space. 4. Safety and order: traffic safety hazards shall be reduced through facility layout, engineering, and management measures, with particular emphasis on protecting vulnerable road users such as pedestrians and cyclists, and ensuring orderly traffic flow. 5. Figure 4.3-4 Example of Walkway Lights 4.3.3 Pavement Surfacing 1. Sidewalk paving: It shall meet the requirements of stability, anti-slip performance, flatness, ecological environmental protection, and urban landscape. Its design shall be practical, economical, aesthetically pleasing, and durable, and shall be designed for permeability in accordance with sponge city requirements. Guidance and directional signs may be added to the paving; signs shall be appropriately scaled and clearly informative. 2. Tactile paving: The color of tactile paving should contrast with the color of adjacent sidewalk paving and be coordinated with the surrounding landscape. The surface of tactile paving profiles shall have anti-slip functionality. The width should be 0.3 m–0.6 m, and the tactile pattern shall protrude 4 mm above the road surface. Tactile paving shall be laid continuously and shall avoid obstacles such as trees (tree pits), utility poles, and guy wires. Figure 4.3-5 Example of tactile paving 3. Curb stones: These shall be designed in accordance with road class, construction scale, landscape environment, and usage requirements. Sidewalks must be provided with curb ramps at all intersections and at the entrances/exits of residential communities and institutions fronting the street. The height difference between the curb stone and the road surface shall not exceed 1 cm. At pedestrian crossings, the centerline of the curb-ramp opening should align with the centerline of the crosswalk. At road intersections, curb ramps are recommended to adopt a full-width, single-sided ramp descending to the bottom. 4. Tree pits / tree grates: Their dimensions shall be designed in coordination with the sidewalk paving, forming a certain proportional modular relationship. The paved surface of the tree pit / tree grate should be flush with the sidewalk paving. Tree grates should preferably use fiberglass grating, eco-friendly rubber, stone paving, and similar materials. In parks, squares, commercial pedestrian streets, and other leisure activity areas, tree pits should be designed in combination with seating, or as compact / multifunctional designs that provide seating functions. Figure 4.3-6 Example of tree pits / tree grates 5. Manhole covers: All types of manhole covers shall comply with the relevant standards in Manhole Covers (GB/T 23858-2009). The paved surface of the manhole cover shall be flush with the sidewalk paving surface, and the height difference shall not exceed 1 cm. Concealed manhole covers may be used; the decorative surface layer shall be unified with the road paving. Manhole covers with distinctive patterns may also be used.
